title: The eve
hook: both armies camped; the conch shells; Arjuna's hands shake

segments.voice: Yesterday: Krishna the negotiator, five villages, and not even a needle's point of land. Your line was five villages. Did you make one small, fair offer? Day seventy-six.

The night before something big. The exam, the surgery, the wedding, the first day. You lie awake and the whole thing plays in your head. A wide plain in north India, called Kurukshetra. Two armies camped on it, bigger than any the world had seen, the story says: kings from every corner of the land, elephants, chariots, horses, foot soldiers stretching to the horizon. Tomorrow cousins will fight cousins. Far away in the palace, the blind king Dhritarashtra can't see any of it. So he asks his charioteer, Sanjaya, who has been given the gift of seeing the battlefield from afar, to tell him what's happening.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `KURUKSHETRA: TWO ARMIES.` → `THE BLIND KING ASKS.`

segments.voice: His question is the very first line of the Bhagavad Gita. In Sanskrit it begins: dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah. On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered, eager to fight: what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Notice what he calls it. Not just a battlefield. A field of dharma. The Gita, which we'll read line by line in a later camp, begins here. Sanjaya tells him. The grandfather Bhishma, commander of the Kaurava army, blows his conch shell, a sound like a lion's roar. Then the other side answers. Krishna, who has agreed to drive Arjuna's chariot, lifts his conch, named Panchajanya. Arjuna blows his, named Devadatta, the god-given. Bhima blows a huge one. Conch after conch, until the sound shakes the sky and the earth. Then Arjuna says to Krishna: drive my chariot out between the two armies. I want to see who I'm fighting. So Krishna drives into the empty space in the middle. And Arjuna looks. And there, on the other side, he sees his grandfather Bhishma, who raised him. His teacher Drona, who taught him to shoot. His uncles, his cousins, his friends' sons. And the greatest archer in the world starts to shake. In the Gita's words, as closely as we can put them: his limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, his skin burns, his hair stands on end, and his great bow slips from his hand. He can't fight. He sits down in the chariot. And that's where Camp 2 leaves him, on the eve.
screen: `ON THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` · `THE CONCH SHELLS ANSWER EACH OTHER.` · `DRIVE ME BETWEEN THE ARMIES.` · `THE BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice your hands. Are they calm or restless? Think of something you're on the eve of: a conversation, a decision, a change, a hard day tomorrow. Let yourself feel what Arjuna feels, if it's there. The dry mouth, the heavy limbs. Don't push it away. It's allowed. Arjuna's fear is where the Gita begins, not where it ends. Now just breathe with it. Slow in, slower out. Let your hands rest open. You don't have to be ready yet. It's only the night before. The bell holds the time.
The eve. Two armies on the field of dharma, the conches sounding, and the greatest archer in the world with shaking hands.
Your line: the night before. Tonight, if something big is coming, let yourself be scared of it for one honest minute, then rest. Day seventy-six.

howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita, which opens on this scene, is recited daily by many Hindus, often chapter by chapter; the conch shell is still blown in temples and homes at the start of worship.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. the conches have sounded. what do you ask your charioteer to do?
options: drive out between the two armies.
fork.reveal: he asks Krishna to drive into the middle so he can see who he's fighting, and seeing his grandfather and teacher, he can't lift his bow.

original.note: Sanskrit: shankha, the conch shell, blown in battle and still blown in worship.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita is a book of wise sayings.
what it means: it opens on a battlefield at dawn, with a hero too frightened and grieved to fight.
what a scholar hears: dharmakshetre kurukshetre: the Gita's first words call the battlefield a field of dharma. it sits inside the Mahabharata's Bhishma Parva.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1:21–30 (between the armies; Arjuna's limbs fail and his bow slips)

notes: Gita 1:1 is quoted in simplified transliteration (dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ); the English that follows is the writer's own plain rendering, not a quotation. Confirm.
Arjuna's symptoms (1:28–30) are paraphrased 'as closely as we can put them'; confirm.
Sanjaya's gift of sight from Vyasa is described as 'the gift of seeing the battlefield from afar'. Confirm.
